title: Grandma's Secret Garden
summary: Hugo and Lucía arrive bored to spend the summer in the countryside. Until, behind the ivy on a wall, they find a blue door that has been shut for years.

scenes.text:
The bus dropped Hugo and Lucía off in front of Grandma Rosa's house, at the end of a dirt track.

Grandma came out to meet them and hugged them so tight that Lucía's hat went crooked.

Hugo looked around. There was no television. There was no tablet. There wasn't even any signal for the phone.

"So what do you do here?" he asked, dropping his backpack.

"Here you look, you listen and you wait," said Grandma, with a wink.

Hugo thought this was going to be the longest, most boring summer of his whole life.

He didn't know yet how right he was. Or in what a strange way.

The first two days went by as slowly as snails. Hugo counted the cracks in the ceiling. Lucía gave a name to every hen.

On the third day, boredom took them all the way to the bottom of the yard, where nobody ever went.

There stood an old, tall stone wall, covered in ivy so thick it looked like a green blanket.

"It's just a wall," said Hugo.

But just then, down from the mountain came a gust of wind.

It stirred the ivy as if the wall were breathing. And underneath, for a moment, they saw something blue.

Lucía reached out and pushed. Behind the leaves there was no stone.

There was wood.

Hugo began pulling the ivy aside with both hands, fast, while Lucía held it back so it wouldn't close again.

Underneath appeared a door.

It was rounded at the top, just the right size for a child and a grandma. It was painted blue, although the blue had been peeling away for years. It had a rusty iron bolt.

"Do you think it's locked?" whispered Lucía.

Hugo pushed with his shoulder. He counted to three.

And the wood swung open with a long groan.

On the other side, surrounded by high walls, there was a garden. A whole garden, hidden from the world, where nobody had set foot for a long, long time.

But it wasn't a garden like the ones in stories.

It was dry. The weeds came up to Lucía's waist. The rose bushes were grey sticks with thorns. In the middle there was a stone fountain, full of dead leaves instead of water.

And everything was so still, so very still, that you couldn't hear a single bird.

"It's dead," Hugo said quietly.

Behind them they heard footsteps.

It was Grandma Rosa, with her apron on and her eyes shining.

"So you found it," she said. "Your grandpa and I planted this garden, a very long time ago. When he passed away, I couldn't bring myself to come in any more. And weeds don't wait for anyone."

She stood looking at the fountain for a long while, without saying anything.

"What if we wake it up?" asked Lucía.

Grandma smiled slowly, as if that question had been waiting for years behind the ivy.

The next morning, Grandma gave them two pairs of old gloves and a bucket.

They worked all week. They pulled up weeds until their arms ached. They gathered stones. They swept up leaves.

When the earth was finally dark and clean, Grandma taught them how to sow.

"With your finger, like this. A little hole. The seed goes in. And you cover it up with love, not with force."

Hugo looked at the seed in his hand. It was the size of a breadcrumb.

"And a sunflower comes out of this? Really?"

"Really. But not today."

They watered, and the earth drank slowly.

"Grandma, nothing's happening," said Hugo, on his knees, staring at the exact spot.

"Yes, it is," she said. "Down below, where we can't see. A garden works best when nobody hurries it."

The days turned into a lovely habit. Get up early. Water. Look. Wait.

Hugo, who before couldn't last five minutes without his phone, spent whole mornings sitting next to his little patch of earth.

Until one day, Lucía shouted so loudly that Grandma came out of the kitchen with a spoon in her hand.

"It's here! It's here!"

In the earth there was a green thread, bent like an elbow, pushing upwards.

Hugo crouched down until his nose was a finger away from the ground.

"It's my sunflower," he said, and his voice wobbled a little.

"It's your patience," said Grandma. "The sunflower is just its way of saying hello."

In the middle of August, the sky changed colour.

First came a different kind of air, bending all the branches the same way. Then came the smell of rain.

And then, right over the house, rumbled the thunder.

It rained as if someone had tipped over a giant bucket. The children watched through the window, their hands pressed against the cold glass.

"The garden!" shouted Hugo.

"Nobody goes out in a storm," said Grandma, calmly, putting her arms around both of them. "Rain is part of the garden too. We'll see tomorrow."

It was the longest night of the summer. Lucía fell asleep on Grandma's shoulder. But Hugo stayed awake, thinking of his green thread, out there all alone, holding out against the water with all its strength.

At dawn, as soon as the rain stopped, the three of them went through the blue door in pyjamas and boots.

The garden was a mess. There were puddles everywhere, and the new plants were lying flat in the mud.

Hugo felt like crying. But Grandma was already on her knees.

"This one isn't broken, look. It's just fallen over."

With a little stick and a piece of string, she tied up a bent stem and stood it up straight again.

Lucía dug channels with her hands so the water could drain away. Hugo lifted the plants one by one, slowly, the way you lift someone who has fallen asleep.

They worked all morning, muddy up to their elbows. Of the ten sunflowers, eight were still alive.

And when they had finished, over the wall flew the very first bee.

On the last Sunday of the summer, the garden wasn't the same any more. And neither were they.

Eight tall sunflowers looked at the sun like curious faces. There were daisies by the fountain, which now had real water in it. And the blue door didn't hide any more: Grandma had left it open on purpose.

When evening came, they brought out three chairs and a blanket.

"Grandma," said Hugo, yawning. "I know what the garden's secret is."

"What is it?"

"You don't hurry it. You stay."

Grandma stroked his hair and said nothing, because sometimes silence is the best answer.

A little while later, the brother and sister were asleep under the blanket, with the smell of earth on their hands and a whole summer tucked away in their hearts.
